# 1.1 Population and Demography

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Demography** is the study of the size, structure, growth, distribution, and movement of a population.

## World population clusters

| Cluster | Region |
|---|---|
| **Major** | **East Asia** — China, Japan (the Tokaido corridor), Korea |
| **Major** | **South Asia** — India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka |
| **Major** | **Europe** — the UK through western Russia |
| **Secondary** | Southeast Asia, northeastern USA |

Nearly all of these are **temperate, low-lying, well-watered, and coastal or riverine** — the conditions for intensive agriculture, and now for trade.

## The demographic measures

| Measure | Definition | Calculation |
|---|---|---|
| **CBR** — Crude Birth Rate | Live births per 1,000 population per year | (births ÷ population) × 1,000 |
| **CDR** — Crude Death Rate | Deaths per 1,000 population per year | (deaths ÷ population) × 1,000 |
| **TFR** — Total Fertility Rate | Average children a woman has in her lifetime | — |
| **ASFR** — Age-Specific Fertility Rate | Live births per 1,000 women in a specific age group per year | — |
| **IMR** — Infant Mortality Rate | Infant (under 1 year) deaths per 1,000 live births | (infant deaths ÷ live births) × 1,000 |
| **NIR** — Natural Increase Rate | Population growth **excluding migration** | (CBR − CDR) ÷ 10, as an annual % |
| **MMR** — Maternal Mortality Ratio | Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births | — |

**What raises and lowers each:**

- **TFR falls** with **female empowerment**, contraception, economic pressure, and changing norms
- **Birth rates fall** with **economic development, female education, contraception access, urbanisation**, and the **high cost of raising children**
- **Death rates fall** with **medical advances, public health, nutrition**, and living standards
- **IMR falls** with **prenatal and postnatal care, immunisation, nutrition, hygiene**, and education

The single most consistent predictor of falling fertility is **female education**. It operates through several channels at once — later marriage, better access to contraception, higher opportunity cost of childbearing — which is why it appears in almost every list above.

**Which measure shows the greatest health disparity between LDCs and MDCs — CBR, CDR, or TFR?**

**None of them: the maternal mortality ratio.** The gap in maternal deaths between rich and poor countries is far larger, proportionally, than the gap in any other common measure — because maternal death is almost entirely preventable with basic obstetric care, so its rate reflects health-system quality more directly than any other statistic.

## Dependency ratios

The **dependency ratio** measures the proportion of **non-working-age people** (children and elderly) to **working-age** people, highlighting the potential economic pressure on those who work.

**High dependency ratio:** a larger proportion of dependents, meaning more economic pressure on the working-age population through taxes and family support.

**Youth dependency ratio** — people aged 0–14 relative to those aged 15–64. It indicates the burden of supporting children through **education, healthcare, and family services**.

**Elderly (old-age) dependency ratio** — people aged 65 and over relative to those aged 15–64. It indicates the burden of **pensions, healthcare**, and other needs of a retired population.

Splitting the ratio matters because the two halves have opposite time signatures. A high **youth** ratio is temporary and becomes an economic advantage when that cohort reaches working age; a high **elderly** ratio is permanent and grows.

## The Demographic Transition Model

| Stage | Name | Birth rate | Death rate | Growth | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | High Stationary | High | High | Stable or slow | Pre-industrial societies, e.g. 18th-century Europe |
| **2** | Early Expanding | High (25+/1,000) | **Falling** (~15/1,000) | **Rapid** | Britain 1750s–late 19th c.; Bangladesh, Nigeria today |
| **3** | Late Expanding | **Falling** | Low | Slowing | Industrialising economies |
| **4** | Low Stationary | Low | Low | Stable | Developed economies |

**Stage 2 is where the population explosion happens**, and the cause is asymmetric timing: **death rates fall first** — through improved sanitation, food production and storage, medical advances, and lower infant mortality — while birth rates take a generation or more to adjust. The gap between the two curves is the growth.

### Key assumptions of the DTM

1. **Linear progression** — all countries follow the same path from Stage 1 to Stage 4 as they develop economically
2. **Industrialisation-driven** — declining death and birth rates are tied to technological and social advancement
3. **No migration impact** — the model ignores migration's role entirely

All three are questionable, and the exam will reward saying so. The model was built from European experience and assumes every country repeats it.

### Stage 5?

Some scholars propose a **Stage 5 (post-industrial decline)**, in which **birth rates fall below death rates**, causing a natural **decrease** in population. Examples include **Japan, Germany, and Italy**, where deaths exceed births but total population is often maintained by **immigration**.

**Criticism:** because the DTM does not account for migration, Stage 5 remains debated — the countries in question are shrinking naturally but not actually shrinking.

### Relating the DTM to population pyramids

Each stage has a characteristic pyramid shape: a **wide-based triangle** in Stages 1–2 (many children, few elderly), a **narrowing base** in Stage 3, and a **column or inverted shape** in Stage 4–5 as the elderly cohort grows and the base contracts.

## Demographic momentum

A **large young population** produces **high demographic momentum**: even after fertility falls to replacement level, the population **continues growing for decades**, because a large cohort of young people is still entering childbearing age.

This is why fertility policy takes so long to show results, and why a country can have below-replacement fertility and a growing population at the same time.

## Malthus

Malthus argued that **population grows geometrically** (2, 4, 8, 16…) while **food supply grows arithmetically** (2, 4, 6, 8…). The imbalance would lead to:

- **Positive checks** — famine and disease
- **Preventative checks** — late marriage

**Criticism:**

- **Technological advances**, notably the **Green Revolution**, disproved his food-scarcity predictions
- He **ignored global trade** and the role of **family planning** in population control

Malthus's arithmetic was not wrong; his assumption that agricultural output could not grow faster than linearly was. That is the standard shape of failed predictions in this field — the logic holds and the premise about technology does not.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Demography** | The study of the size, structure, growth, distribution, and movement of a population |
| **CBR (Crude Birth Rate)** | Live births per 1,000 population per year |
| **CDR (Crude Death Rate)** | Deaths per 1,000 population per year |
| **TFR (Total Fertility Rate)** | Average children a woman has in her lifetime |
| **ASFR (Age-Specific Fertility Rate)** | Live births per 1,000 women in a specific age group per year |
| **IMR (Infant Mortality Rate)** | Infant (under 1 year) deaths per 1,000 live births |
| **NIR (Natural Increase Rate)** | Population growth excluding migration, calculated as (CBR − CDR) ÷ 10 and given as an annual percentage |
| **MMR (Maternal Mortality Ratio)** | Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births |
| **Dependency ratio** | The proportion of non-working-age people (children and elderly) to working-age people, highlighting the potential economic pressure on those who work |
| **High dependency ratio** | A larger proportion of dependents, meaning more economic pressure on the working-age population through taxes and family support |
| **Youth dependency ratio** | People aged 0–14 relative to those aged 15–64; it indicates the burden of supporting children through education, healthcare, and family services |
| **Elderly (old-age) dependency ratio** | People aged 65 and over relative to those aged 15–64; it indicates the burden of pensions, healthcare, and other needs of a retired population |
| **Stage 1: High Stationary** | High birth rate, high death rate, stable or slow growth — pre-industrial societies |
| **Stage 2: Early Expanding** | High birth rate (25+/1,000) with a falling death rate (~15/1,000), giving rapid growth |
| **Stage 3: Late Expanding** | Falling birth rate, low death rate, slowing growth |
| **Stage 4: Low Stationary** | Low birth rate, low death rate, stable population — developed economies |
| **Stage 5 (post-industrial decline)** | A proposed stage in which birth rates fall below death rates, causing a natural decrease in population |
| **Demographic momentum** | The effect by which a large young population keeps a population growing for decades even after fertility falls to replacement level, because a large cohort is still entering childbearing age |
| **Positive checks** | Famine and disease |
| **Preventative checks** | Late marriage |

# 2.1 Migration

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ravenstein's Laws

Ravenstein derived a set of empirical regularities about migration that still hold reasonably well:

1. **Most migration is over a short distance.** Migrants tend to move short distances, often within the same region or country.
2. Migration proceeds **step by step**, in stages, rather than in one long move.
3. **Long-distance migrants** head for the **great centres of commerce and industry**.
4. Each migration flow produces a **counter-flow** in the opposite direction.
5. **Rural** inhabitants are more migratory than **urban** ones.
6. Within a country, **females** migrate more than males; **internationally**, males predominate.
7. **Most migrants are adults**, not families with children.
8. Large towns grow **more by migration than by natural increase**.
9. Migration **increases with economic development** and improved transport.
10. Migration is **mostly economic** in motive.

Because migrants tend to move short distances and along established routes, **communities of people from the same origin form in the new location** — chain migration, which then makes subsequent migration from that origin easier still.

## Push and pull factors

Migration is analysed as a balance between **push factors** (reasons to leave) and **pull factors** (reasons to come), usually grouped by category:

| Category | Push (reasons to leave) | Pull (reasons to come) |
|---|---|---|
| **Economic** | High unemployment, poverty, low wages | Money, jobs, financial opportunity, higher standard of living |
| **Political** | Persecution, war, oppression | Stability, freedom, safety |
| **Social** | Discrimination, lack of services | Family and community, education, healthcare |
| **Environmental** | Drought, flood, natural disaster, degradation | Favourable climate, fertile land |

Push and pull factors rarely operate alone. The people who leave a country in economic crisis are typically not the poorest — migration costs money — which is one of the reasons development can **increase** emigration in the short term before reducing it.

## The three intervening concepts

Three ideas explain why a push and a pull do not automatically produce a migration:

**Intervening obstacle.** A barrier that makes the journey harder or impossible — a border, a mountain range, a visa requirement, the cost of travel. It considers the **costs and effort involved in making the move**.

**Intervening opportunity.** An attractive place **along a migrant's intended route** that causes them to **stop there instead of reaching the original destination**. This is a large part of why Ravenstein's step migration occurs: migrants aim far and stop when something good enough appears.

**Complementarity.** One place has something another place needs. For migration this usually means one area has a **surplus of people or skills** while another has a **demand for them**. Without complementarity there is no reason for a flow at all, however strong the push.

The three work in sequence: complementarity creates the potential for migration, intervening opportunities redirect it, and intervening obstacles reduce it.

## Brain drain

The migration of skilled professionals from poorer to richer countries **depletes the healthcare workforce in the origin countries**, weakening their health systems and worsening health outcomes.

The dynamic is self-reinforcing and difficult to address: a country that invests in training doctors loses that investment to countries that did not make it, which reduces its capacity to train more. It is one of the clearest cases where an individually rational decision produces a collectively damaging outcome.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Step migration** | Migration that proceeds step by step, in stages, rather than in one long move |
| **Chain migration** | Communities of people from the same origin forming in the new location, which then makes subsequent migration from that origin easier still |
| **Push factors** | Reasons to leave — unemployment, poverty and low wages; persecution, war and oppression; discrimination and lack of services; drought, flood, disaster and degradation |
| **Pull factors** | Reasons to come — money, jobs and a higher standard of living; stability, freedom and safety; family, education and healthcare; favourable climate and fertile land |
| **Intervening obstacle** | A barrier that makes the journey harder or impossible — a border, a mountain range, a visa requirement, the cost of travel; it considers the costs and effort involved in making the move |
| **Intervening opportunity** | An attractive place along a migrant's intended route that causes them to stop there instead of reaching the original destination |
| **Complementarity** | One place has something another place needs — usually one area has a surplus of people or skills while another has a demand for them |
| **Brain drain** | The migration of skilled professionals from poorer to richer countries, which depletes the healthcare workforce in the origin countries, weakening their health systems and worsening health outcomes |

# S1M-1 Chapter 1 (10%)

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Geography H review guide (PA). Writers: Katie Hsieh 10-3. Editor: Katie Hsieh 10-3. Range: chapter 1(10%) +chapter 4+ 5.1. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

3 types of density:

Arithmetic (crude) = total number of ppl/ total land area

Physiological (nutritional) = total number of ppl/ arable land A high physiological density suggests that a region may struggle feeding its population. For example: Egypt’s physiological density is extremely high because nearly all its people depend on the narrow strip of arable land along the Nile.

Agricultural= number of farmers/ arable lands

Developed countries have low agricultural density as only a few farmers using machines work large areas while developing countries often have high agricultural density (many farmers working small plots by hand).

Diffusion processes:

Relocation: physically moving, carrying ideas

Slow, small-scale, and tied to migration patterns.

Contagious Diffusion: rapid, widespread diffusion throughout the population, analogous to the spread of a disease.

Example: A viral internet meme spreading person-to-person.

Stimulus Di usion: The spread of an underlying principle of an idea or innovation, even if the speci c characteristic itself does not spread successfully. The idea is adopted but modi ed to t local conditions. Example: McDonald's adapting its menu to local tastes in di erent countries (e.g., vegetarian options in India)

Hierarchical Di usion: spread of an idea or innovation from persons or nodes of authority or power to other persons or places.

Two Common Patterns: 1. From larger to smaller places: An innovation appears in a major city rst, then spreads to secondary cities, then to towns, and nally to rural areas. 2. From in uential people to the general population.

Absolute location: latitudes 0-90 NS longitudes 0-180 EW

# S1M-2 Chapter 4 Key issue 1

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Geography H review guide (PA). Writers: Katie Hsieh 10-3. Editor: Katie Hsieh 10-3. Range: chapter 1(10%) +chapter 4+ 5.1. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

Folk and popular culture

Culture: -shared practices (birth rituals, death rituals, marriages…)

-technologies (communications, transportation)

-attitudes and behaviours (age of maturity, gender roles)

Nonmaterial culture: intangible concepts, ideas, and behavioral norms that shape a group’s identity, such as religions, beliefs, customs, oral traditions, songs…

Material culture: refers to physical objects and tangible items such as architecture, housing, clothing, food…

Habit: a repetitive act performed by an individual

Custom: A habit widely adopted by a group, such as celebrating a holiday.

Culture: a group’s entire collection of customs

Folk culture

Origin: typically anonymous, with unknown dates and originators; may have multiple independent hearths in isolated locations.

Diffusion: diffuses slowly and on a small scale, usually through relocation diffusion; changes over space

Distribution: clustered in specific, often rural or isolated areas, strongly influenced by local physical and cultural factors. EXAMPLE: distinct folk painting traditions are distributed within the Himalayas as a result of isolation of cultural groups. (Buddhists—divine figures, Hindus —domestic everyday scenes, Muslims—plants and flowers, animists—symbols)

Popular culture

Origin: originates at the hearth, a node of innovation. Usually traceable to a specific person or corporation, often in developed countries.

Diffusion: diffuses rapidly, typically through hierarchical diffusion, aided by modern technology, changes over time

Distribution: widespread across many countries with little regard for environments; main obstacle is income

MUSIC

Folk: originated anonymously and transmitted orally. Content from events in daily life and life cycle events.

Popular: written by specific individuals, purpose of being sold or performed to people. Displays a high degree of technical skill through electronic equipment.

SPORTS

SOCCER (folk to popular culture)

Origin: folk culture. In England during the 1000s, after the danish invasion, workers encountered a danish soldier’s head, which they began to kick. And this was imitated by boys, resembling mob scenes. It was not legalized until 1603 by king James I.

Diffusion: popular culture. 1800s, football was founded in the UK, by churches to provide factory workers with organized recreation during leisure hours, and then became a subject taught. Increasing leisure time permitted people to participate and view which started association football around the world.

SURVIVING FOLK SPORTS

Cricket, wushu, baseball…

Key issue 2: distribution of MATERIAL CULTURE

Clothing

Folk clothing:

Primarily responds to environmental conditions and cultural values.

It must adapt to local climate and agricultural practices, and in some places it also depends on religious practices.

EXAMPLES: fur-lined boots in Arctic climates to protect against the cold; Burqa and chador worn by women following folk customs in southwest Asia and north africa, while in European countries, women are prohibited from wearing bu

burqa in public as it represents unacceptable treatment of women as second-class citizens.

Popular clothing:

Style differences primarily reflect time rather than place.

It is primarily influenced by occupation and income level.

For example, business professionals wear suits; factory workers wear work clothes.

Diffuses through mass production and fashion industry chains by improved communications

Food

Folk food:

Depends on local environment, availability of products

Concept of Terroir refers to the unique flavor imparted to food (such as wine) by a region’s soil, climate or other physical features.

Some foods are eaten as it are perceived to enhance qualities considered desirable by society (for eg. Abipone people eat jaguars, stags, bulls to make them strong, believed to make people cowardly)

Taboos: prohibitions on foods. For example, Islamic and Jewish prohibitions on pork, hindu avoidance of cattle.

EXAMPLES: In Asia, rice is grown in milder, moister regions, while wheat thrives in colder drier regions. In Northern Europe, abundant wood supply encouraged slow stewing and roasting of foods over fire, which also provided home heat in the colder climate.

Popular food:

Globalization and homogenization.

Driven by mass media and multinational corporations

EXAMPLE: cola preferences are influenced by politics in Russia, while its influenced by religion in south west Asia.

Wine production: environmental factors—Climate, topography, Soil

Cultural factors—religions (hindus and muslims avoid alcoholic beverages)

Housing

Folk housing:

Responds to environment and culture (building materials)

1. New England: boxed shaped with a central hall

2. Middle Atlantic: “I houses”

3. Lower chesapeake/ southern tidewater: steep roofs and chimneys

Sacred spaces

Popular housing:

Modern housing styles are influenced by improved communications and commercialized building materials.

Postmodernism (Geography/Urban Context): It rejects the modernist pursuit of grand theories, universal laws, and a single truthNeomodernism

Neomodernism: ”replacing" postmodernism, but it does not simply return to modernism—it reinterprets or continues certain themes of modernism under new conditions.

Vajrayana Theravada Mahayana

Key issue 3: ACCESS

Obstacle to popular culture= lack of access to electronic media (TV)

Diffusion of TV: developed-developing countries

Diffusion of internet: similar to TV but more rapid

Diffusion of Social media

CHALLENGES IN ACCESSING

External threat: developed countries controlled the media (Japan UK US)

Many satellites and cable providers in developing countries block offending networks, avoiding traditional folk cultures

Internal threat: governments limit access to the internet and TV.

Key issue 4: Sustainability

Globalization creates sustainability problems for folk culture (struggles to keep unique local traditions) and popular culture (struggles with uniform, unsustainable practices).

Folk Culture Challenges

- Globalization + spread of popular culture make it hard to preserve old, unique local customs.

- Rising incomes make people want popular culture goods; they may abandon traditional folk values.

- Diffusion of popular culture from wealthy countries can push Western ideas over local folk culture.

EXAMPLE: Amish folk culture

Origin: 1600s Swiss Mennonite group (Jakob Ammann) fled Europe for religious freedom.

Migration to North America: two main waves (early 1700s to Pennsylvania; early 1800s to Ohio, Illinois, Iowa, Canada) looking for cheap land.

Cultural traits: Reject most modern electrical/mechanical technology; use horse & buggy, hand farming tools, distinctive clothing, unique religious/farming customs.

Distribution: Spread across rural US (mostly Northeast/Midwest), slow diffusion by migration; isolated communities keep their folk identity separate from mainstream American culture.

Land pressure problem: Traditional Amish custom gives each adult son a farm. Farmland in Lancaster County, PA is expensive and scarce near cities.

Solution: Many Amish sell their Pennsylvania land and move to Kentucky, where farmland is cheaper.

Conflict with popular culture: Tourism brings outsiders to view their folk culture; this forces the Amish into contact with popular culture.

Marriage in India:

Dowry definition: Originally a gift from the bride’s family to the groom’s family as a sign of respect. Historically, it was small, to support the new bride.

Cultural shift: Over time, the custom reversed. Families now expect a large, expensive dowry (cash, cars, electronics, appliances). Dowries became a major income source for the groom’s family.

Government action: India banned dowries in 1961, but the law is widely ignored.

Harm/violence: If the bride’s family cannot pay the promised dowry, the bride may be abused, abandoned, or killed. Statistics show thousands of dowry-related deaths and abuse cases each year.

Popular Culture Challenges

Landscape pollution and depletion of scarce natural resources.

1. Landscape Pollution

Reshapes land without caring about local climate, soil, or ecosystems to create a uniform landscape—Developers flatten hills, fill valleys, and use the same landscaping materials anywhere.

- Uniform look = instant product recognition, easier consumption.

- Examples:

- Fast food franchises: built for familiarity for travelers; new visitors feel comfortable.

- Golf courses: large areas (200 acres). They require reshaping the land.

- Environmental Capacity

- The environment can only absorb a limited amount of human waste

- Popular culture creates huge amounts of solid waste (cans, plastic, paper, old cars). Many of these items are thrown away, not recycled.

resource depletion

demand for animal product: require large amount of certain animals resulting in depletion or even extinction. EXAMPLE: fur for clothings, increased meat consumption.

recycling of resources:3 Recycling Collection Systems

- Curbside programs: Recyclables picked up at homes (most common)
- Drop-off centers: People bring waste to special sites
- Buy-back centers/deposit programs: You get money back for returning containers

Cultural landscape:

Physical features

Agriculture and industry

Religions and linguistics

sequent occupance: groups throughout history that leave their marks on a place

e.g., New York City

Native American groups populated the shores of New York Harbor, which were rich in oysters and other seafood the city was controlled by the Dutch (place-names like Harlem)

The city was controlled by the Dutch (place-names like

under British colonial rule (place-names such asGreenwich Village, Williamsburg, and the borough of Queens)

Traditional modern architecture

Land use patterns

Preserve folk culture

eg: Amish, Jewish, Chinese

Hebrew—Israel according to the laws the child's first language must be Hebrew

Cultural trait: A single, distinguishing feature of regular occurrence within a culture, such as using chopsticks.

Cultural complex: A related set of cultural traits describing one aspect of a society's behavior or activity. For example: Americans love cars.

Cultural system: Multiple cultural complexes share common traits (such as ethnicity, language, religion), forming a larger system. For example, the Amish.

Acculturation: a group adopts part of the host society's culture but does not completely lose its own traits.

Assimilation: A group's cultural traits are altered to resemble those of another group, and the immigrant group blends into the host culture, losing many distinctive traits.

Cultural syncretism: cultural blending, e.g., Day of the dead

Cultural relativism: An approach to understanding other cultures that seeks to understand individuals and cultures from a broader perspective of their own cultural logic.

Cultural ethnocentrism: Judging another culture solely by the values and standards of one's own culture.

Ethnic enclave: A place with a high concentration of an ethnic group that is distinct from those in the surrounding area. It can serve as an example of "spatial clustering" in urban settlement. Eg: Little India

# S1M-3 Chapter 5.1 Distribution of languages

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Geography H review guide (PA). Writers: Katie Hsieh 10-3. Editor: Katie Hsieh 10-3. Range: chapter 1(10%) +chapter 4+ 5.1. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

- Literary tradition: a system of written communication.

- Language family: Largest group. Languages share an ancient common ancestor, from way before recorded history.

- Language branch: Within one family. Shared ancestor thousands of years ago; differences are smaller than between separate families.

- Language group: Within one branch. Shared origin in the recent past; similar grammar & vocabulary.

- Estimates 6,909 languages worldwide.

- Only 11 languages (English, Mandarin, Spanish, Arabic, Hindi, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Japanese, Lahnda, German) are widely known.\

Language families

Indo-European

The most widely used language family

Main distribution: Europe, South Asia, North America, Latin America

Sino-Tibetan

Main area: China + several Southeast Asian countries

Mandarin—most used

Other large Sinitic languages (≥20 million speakers): Wu, Min, Yue (Cantonese), Jinyu, Xiang, Hakka, Gan → Mostly in southern & eastern China

- Chinese uses logograms: symbols that represent words/ideas, not sounds

ASIAN LANG FAMILIES

Austronesian

Distribution: Indonesia, Madagascar, Pacific islands

Javanese—most widely used in Indonesia

- Many languages here have long history of seafaring migration.

Austro-Asiatic

Main language: Vietnamese

- Uses the Roman alphabet modified with diacritics (accents/tone marks) → adapted from Catholic missionaries.

- Main location: Vietnam, Cambodia.

Tai-Kadai

- Mainly in Southeast Asia (Thailand, Laos).

- Thai is the major language.

- Uses logograms historically (similar idea to Chinese writing), now its script is different.

Japanese

Korean

Languages of SW Asia and N africa and central asia

Uralic

European non-Indo-European family.

- Languages: Finnish, Hungarian, Estonian.

- Origin: Central Asia; migrated to Europe long ago.

- These are surrounded by Indo-European languages but kept their own language identity.

Altaic

- Main: Turkish, Mongolian.

- Turkish switched from Arabic script to Latin alphabet

- Once spread across Central Asia.

African Language Families

1. Afro-Asiatic

Southwest Asia + North Africa

- Biggest language: Arabic

- Arabic is the main language of Islam; one of the UN official languages.

- Hebrew also belongs to Afro-Asiatic.

2. Niger-Congo

Largest African language family by number of languages

- Covers most of sub-Saharan Africa.

- Famous language: Swahili

- Swahili is a lingua franca in East Africa.

- Mix of African languages + Arabic loanwords.

3. Nilo-Saharan

- Small number of speakers, scattered across north-central Africa.

- Languages are not widely used.

4. Khoisan

- Famous for click consonants — unique clicking sounds.

- Very few speakers today; endangered
